title: Inventory & reservations
summary: Build products, locations, stock movements, and reservations that remain correct under concurrency.
outcome: A second full-stack app where the last item cannot be reserved twice and retries cannot duplicate stock changes.
prerequisites: Finish Support-ticket app and the transaction/idempotency milestones. Use a disposable PostgreSQL database for race experiments.
model: Product: id, sku (unique within owner), name, archivedAt. Location: id, ownerId, name.
Stock: productId, locationId, onHand, reserved; unique pair and constraints 0 ≤ reserved ≤ onHand.
Reservation: id, operationId, productId, locationId, quantity, status, expiresAt. StockMovement records every accepted stock adjustment.
boundaries: Authenticated command → inventory service → one SQL transaction for conditional stock mutation, reservation, and receipt. Read availability is advisory until the write commits.

milestones.title: Build the catalog and stock ledger
milestones.brief: Implement product/location CRUD and auditable stock adjustments with integer quantities.
milestones.explanation: A schema catches bad input early; a database constraint protects stored truth under every writer. Use integer quantities for indivisible items and choose an explicit unit/precision policy for measured goods. A stock adjustment is a command with a reason, not an arbitrary overwrite of a displayed total.
steps: Define product SKU uniqueness, archival behavior, location ownership, and positive integer adjustment quantities. Add SQL constraints and foreign keys.
Build product/location forms, lists, and archive actions. Implement stock receipt and removal commands with an actor and reason.
Write the balance change and stock movement in one transaction. Reject removal below reserved stock and test direct SQL constraint violations in a disposable database.

checks.label: Duplicate scoped SKUs, fractional quantities, and invalid relationships are rejected.
Stock balances and movement records agree after accepted adjustments.
Archived catalog entries preserve history and cannot receive disallowed new operations.

milestones.experiment: Try removing five items when only three unreserved items remain. Inspect balance and ledger to confirm neither changed.
milestones.review: Explain why UI validation and an integer TypeScript annotation cannot replace database constraints.
milestones.stretch: Support moving stock between locations with an atomic debit, credit, and paired movement records.

milestones.title: Reserve the last item safely
milestones.brief: Make two concurrent reservation requests compete for one remaining item without overselling.
milestones.explanation: Reading available=1 and later writing reserved=1 is unsafe when two requests race. Perform a conditional update or acquire appropriate row locks inside the transaction. Treat insufficient stock as a domain failure. If the database requires transaction retries, retry the complete transaction within a bound.
steps: Define availability as onHand minus reserved and write the accepted/rejected reservation responses before implementing them.
Atomically increment reserved only when sufficient stock remains, then insert the reservation in the same transaction. Use consistent lock order for multi-row operations.
Launch two requests concurrently against PostgreSQL with one item available. Inspect both responses, reservation rows, and final balances.

checks.label: Exactly one of two competing requests reserves the last item.
No committed balance has reserved greater than onHand or below zero.
A reservation insertion failure rolls back the stock update.

milestones.experiment: Use a barrier so both clients begin together. A sequential test cannot demonstrate protection against this race.
milestones.review: Show the exact SQL predicate or locking strategy. An in-process mutex does not protect against a second server instance.
milestones.stretch: Reserve a basket across multiple products and demonstrate all-or-nothing allocation with consistent lock ordering.

milestones.title: Retry, release, and expire reservations
milestones.brief: Finish the reservation lifecycle with duplicate-safe requests and single-application release or expiry.
milestones.explanation: A reservation can leave active state once. Release, fulfilment, and expiration may race; guard the transition and stock update in one transaction. Durable receipts make a retried request return its prior result. A worker should not decrement reserved again for an already released record.
steps: Define active → fulfilled/released/expired transitions. Specify how onHand and reserved change for each and use a controllable clock for expiry tests.
Store a unique operation receipt with each accepted command. Reject reuse with different parameters and test a lost response followed by retry.
Run an expiry worker with bounded batches and clean shutdown. Race user release against expiry, then deploy and verify backup restoration preserves balances and history.

checks.label: Duplicate requests return the established outcome without extra balance changes.
Release and expiry racing each other apply the stock correction only once.
Restored reservations, receipts, movements, and balances satisfy the same invariants.

milestones.experiment: Freeze time just before expiry, start a release, advance time, and run expiry concurrently. Repeat with a dropped response and request retry.
milestones.review: Check receipt uniqueness, retention, transaction scope, and worker restart behavior. Reconcile the ledger against balances as an independent check.
milestones.stretch: Add reconciliation that reports inconsistencies without silently rewriting stock, and rehearse a repair procedure.

milestones.title: Move stock between locations
milestones.brief: Transfer available stock from one location to another with paired ledger records and no intermediate loss or duplication.
milestones.explanation: A transfer is a single business operation with two balance changes. Check ownership and available quantity, acquire locks in a consistent order, and commit debit, credit, and movements together. Reversing a transfer is a new auditable operation; deleting its history would make later reconciliation harder.
steps: Define transfer identity, source, destination, quantity, actor, and reason. Reject identical locations and cross-owner transfers.
Implement one transaction for both balances and paired movement records. Choose deterministic row lock ordering for concurrent opposite transfers.
Test insufficient availability, a failed destination write, duplicate submission, and two opposing transfers started together.

checks.label: Accepted transfers conserve total on-hand stock.
Any intermediate failure rolls back both balances and ledger records.
Concurrent opposing transfers terminate safely under the retry policy.

milestones.experiment: Run A-to-B and B-to-A transfers concurrently while one location contains reserved stock. Verify both conservation and the reserved-stock invariant.
milestones.review: Explain why two separate successful HTTP updates are insufficient. A timeout after commit also requires the same idempotency policy as other stock commands.
milestones.stretch: Add an in-transit state for physical movements whose dispatch and receipt occur at different times.

milestones.title: Reconcile a physical stock count
milestones.brief: Record a physical count without blindly overwriting stock movements that happened while the count was being performed.
milestones.explanation: A count is an observation taken at a particular time or ledger position. If stock moves during counting, the observed number cannot simply replace the latest balance. Define a freeze, snapshot, or reconciliation policy, then make the adjustment an explicit, authorized ledger event with supporting evidence.
steps: Model count session, scope, observed quantity, baseline revision, counter, and approval status. Decide which movements are permitted during counting.
Compute proposed adjustments against the declared baseline and show them before approval. Require a revision check or recalculation if relevant stock has changed.
Test receipts and reservations during a count, rejected approval, duplicate approval, and a count lower than currently reserved stock.

checks.label: Intervening stock movements are never silently discarded.
Approved adjustments have an actor, reason, and count-session link.
The resulting balances satisfy reserved and nonnegative constraints.

milestones.experiment: Count ten items, receive five more before approval, then apply the count. Explain why a naive overwrite to ten would lose a valid receipt.
milestones.review: Distinguish observed quantity from a command to set current balance. Record the business choice for disputed counts instead of inventing certainty.
milestones.stretch: Require a second person to approve unusually large discrepancies and test that approval cannot be self-granted.

milestones.title: Measure correctness under contention
milestones.brief: Run a bounded load experiment that measures latency and errors while independently checking stock invariants and ledger agreement.
milestones.explanation: A fast response is not useful if the final state is wrong. Define a workload with competing reservations, releases, and transfers, then verify the resulting data independently of the request handlers. Report percentiles, rejection categories, and database contention together; expected out-of-stock responses are not the same as infrastructure failures.
steps: Seed a disposable dataset and specify client count, duration, request mix, and starting balances. Establish a low-load baseline first.
Run increasing bounded concurrency, recording durations and categorized outcomes. Inspect lock waits and query plans before changing the code.
After each run, reconcile balances, active reservations, receipts, and movements. Repeat after one targeted change and compare both performance and correctness.

checks.label: Every run ends with valid balances and reconcilable ledger totals.
Reports separate business rejections from technical failures.
Performance claims include workload, environment, and before/after measurements.

milestones.experiment: Disable a revision guard in a disposable branch. Verify that your independent invariant check catches the resulting corruption even if request latency improves.
milestones.review: Avoid selecting only the fastest successful requests. Keep the failure rate and workload constant enough that before/after results remain comparable.
milestones.stretch: Add a rollback rehearsal after deploying the measured optimization and verify that old code still reads the resulting records.
